query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small microalloying addition of molybdenum (≈1–2 at%) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its practical performance by forming uniformly distributed nanoscale Mo-rich precipitates that enhance resistance to room-temperature creep and corrosion while maintaining the existing strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a fine, lamellar dual-phase (typically FCC/B2) microstructure that provides good fracture strength and ductility yet falls short in sustained mechanical stability, creep resistance, and corrosion performance under extreme environmental conditions.
generation.intervention: Microalloying by introducing a low concentration (≈1–2 at%) of Mo during the alloy synthesis (melting/casting) process.
generation.conditions: The modified alloy should be processed using conventional casting and controlled heat treatments, and its performance evaluated under cyclic extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading that simulates aircraft/spacecraft fastener conditions, and in corrosive environments representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation and uniform distribution of nanoscale Mo-rich precipitates at grain boundaries and within the lamellar matrix.
generation.mechanism: Low-level Mo addition promotes precipitation during solidification or subsequent heat treatment; these finely dispersed Mo-rich particles impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby enhancing creep resistance, while also contributing to a more stable microstructure and passive film formation that improves corrosion resistance without sacrificing the strength–ductility synergy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the original alloy, the Mo-alloyed samples are expected to exhibit improved resistance to room-temperature creep and lower corrosion rates, while retaining or modestly enhancing yield and ultimate tensile strengths alongside comparable ductility. The exact percentage improvements remain to be quantified experimentally.
generation.baseline: The unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy, which in its as-cast state shows a fine lamellar FCC/B2 structure with good strength and ductility but limited long-term creep and corrosion resistance under extreme operating conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only when Mo is added in a controlled, low concentration (≈1–2 at%) under processing conditions that preserve the fine lamellar microstructure; deviations such as excessive Mo or altered thermal treatments may lead to coarser precipitates or embrittlement, nullifying the intended improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvements in creep resistance and corrosion behavior is uncertain and will need to be established through systematic experimental testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples with varying Mo contents (0, 1, 2, and 3 at%) using identical casting and heat-treatment protocols to promote similar lamellar microstructures. Subject these samples to cyclic extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical creep tests under constant load at both room and elevated temperatures, and corrosion tests in environments simulating aerospace fastener conditions. Compare the mechanical properties and microstructural characteristics with the baseline unalloyed material.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Elongation at fracture
Creep rate and time-to-failure under constant load
Electrochemical corrosion rate and passive film stability
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) for precipitate size and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-alloyed samples do not display a statistically significant improvement in their creep resistance and corrosion behavior, or if the strength–ductility balance is compromised relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of molybdenum (Mo) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will induce the in situ formation of nanoscale Mo‐rich precipitates that improve the alloy's high-temperature creep and corrosion resistance while maintaining its strength–ductility balance.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
drafts.intervention: Microalloying by introducing a low concentration (≈1–2 at%) of Mo during alloy synthesis
drafts.conditions: Testing under cyclic extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, and room-temperature conditions representative of aircraft/spacecraft fastener environments
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation and uniform dispersion of nanoscale Mo-rich precipitates at grain boundaries and within the lamellar matrix
drafts.mechanism: The Mo-rich precipitates are proposed to act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby enhancing creep resistance and stabilizing the microstructure against corrosive degradation while preserving ductility and strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples with optimal Mo addition will demonstrate statistically significant improvements in high-temperature creep resistance and corrosion performance compared to the baseline alloy, without compromising the existing balance between strength and ductility.
drafts.baseline: Performance of the existing AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic alloy, which, despite its fine lamellar structure, does not fully meet industrial standards for creep resistance and corrosion stability under service conditions.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected when Mo is added in a controlled, low concentration (ideally within 1–2 at%), processed under similar thermal treatments; excessive Mo or processing variances could lead to precipitate coarsening or brittleness, deviating from the predicted improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples with varying Mo contents (0, 1, 2, and 3 at%). Apply identical casting and heat treatment procedures to promote the formation of nano-scale precipitates. Subject each set to cyclic thermal loading, long-term mechanical creep tests, and electrochemical corrosion tests, alongside conventional tensile tests.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of creep resistance (creep strain rates and time-to-failure at prescribed stresses and temperatures)
Electrochemical corrosion rates and passive film stability under simulated service environments
Tensile properties including yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (elongation at fracture)
Microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) to assess precipitate size, distribution, and phase interface integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-alloyed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature creep resistance and corrosion performance compared to the baseline alloy, or if the strength–ductility balance is compromised (e.g., significant reduction in ductility), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (~1 at%) of tungsten to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its performance by forming fine tungsten-rich precipitates that stabilize the lamellar microstructure, thereby enhancing resistance to room-temperature creep and corrosion without compromising the alloy’s strength and ductility.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure currently offering good strength and plasticity but insufficient creep and corrosion resistance for aerospace fastener applications.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of approximately 1 atomic percent tungsten into the alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: The modified alloy is prepared using the same processing route as the starting material, with tungsten addition kept near 1 at% to avoid deleterious phase segregation. It is evaluated under operating conditions typical for aerospace applications including extreme temperature fluctuations (up to ~600°C) and long-term mechanical loading in corrosive environments.
drafts.structural_mediator: The tungsten preferentially forms fine tungsten-rich precipitates that pin dislocations and stabilize the lamellar interfaces.
drafts.mechanism: The precipitates act to impede dislocation motion and reduce grain-boundary sliding, thereby improving room-temperature creep resistance. In addition, the tungsten-rich phases contribute to a more stable passive film that enhances corrosion resistance, all while maintaining a balance of strength and ductility.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Enhanced resistance to long-term creep and reduced corrosion rates, with the alloy retaining its high strength and ductility, thereby better meeting industrial and aerospace requirements.
drafts.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy without tungsten addition, which currently shows limitations in sustained mechanical load handling and corrosion resistance.
drafts.boundary: The benefits are expected to emerge only if the tungsten content is maintained at around 1 at% since higher amounts could lead to embrittlement or unfavorable phase changes. The intervention should work within the tested temperature range and mechanical conditions relevant to aerospace fasteners.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two alloy batches: one with standard composition and one with ~1 at% tungsten addition. Use identical processing conditions. Subject both batches to accelerated creep tests (constant load at varying temperatures up to ~600°C) and corrosion evaluations in simulated aerospace environments.
measurements: Quantitative creep rate under constant load over time
Corrosion rate measurements in a representative corrosive environment
Tensile strength and ductility tests
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM, XRD) to verify the presence and distribution of tungsten-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-added alloy does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in creep resistance and corrosion behavior compared to the baseline alloy, or if its ductility is substantially reduced, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Subjecting the as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy to cryogenic rolling followed by a controlled low-temperature annealing step will generate a refined hierarchical microstructure that simultaneously enhances its strength, ductility, and high-temperature stability.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA displaying a fine lamellar FCC/B2 dual-phase structure with good overall mechanical performance that is insufficient for demanding industrial applications and extreme environment requirements.
drafts.intervention: Apply cryogenic rolling (e.g., deformation at liquid nitrogen temperature) followed by annealing at an optimized low temperature (around 700°C) for a short time.
drafts.conditions: Processing to be performed under cryogenic conditions (approximately -196°C) to induce severe plastic deformation and then annealed at a controlled temperature (∼700°C) for a brief duration to enable partial recrystallization without significant grain coarsening.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a hierarchical microstructure featuring ultrafine grains within the original lamellar architecture, increased density of phase boundaries, and potentially dispersed nano-scale precipitates.
drafts.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling induces a high density of dislocations and refines the grain size through severe plastic deformation, while subsequent annealing allows limited recovery and recrystallization. This controlled process further enhances grain-boundary strengthening and maintains phase stability, leading to both higher yield/fracture strength and sustained ductility, as well as improved resistance to high-temperature fluctuations, creep, and corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast alloy, the treated samples are expected to show a significant increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths (e.g., >20% improvement) with at least comparable ductility, alongside enhanced stability under thermal cycling and corrosive environments.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA typically exhibits a fracture stress around 944 MPa and an elongation of approximately 25-26% at room temperature, with performance issues under long-term high-temperature service and environmental stresses.
drafts.boundary: The improvement is contingent on achieving a uniformly deformed microstructure during cryogenic rolling and preventing excessive grain growth during annealing. Inadequate processing control may lead to coarsening or nonuniform strain distribution that could negate the intended benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA samples: one undergoes the proposed cryogenic rolling followed by controlled annealing, and the other is maintained in the as-cast state or processed via conventional room-temperature rolling. Conduct a series of standardized tensile tests, high-temperature stability tests (e.g., creep testing), and corrosion evaluation under simulated extreme environmental conditions.
measurements: Yield strength
Ultimate tensile strength
Elongation to failure
Microstructural analysis (using electron microscopy to assess grain size and phase distribution)
Creep resistance at elevated temperatures
Corrosion rate under simulated corrosive environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryogenically processed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 20% increase in yield strength with maintained ductility) or if high-temperature stability, creep resistance, and corrosion performance are not notably enhanced relative to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a modest microalloying addition of Nb (around 1–2 at%) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will promote the formation of fine, coherent Nb-rich precipitates within the FCC lamellae and along lamellar interfaces, thereby increasing creep resistance and corrosion stability at high and fluctuating temperatures while maintaining or improving the alloy’s strength–ductility balance.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure that already provides a promising combination of high fracture strength and ductility.
drafts.intervention: Modify the alloy composition via a targeted Nb microalloying (~1–2 at% substitution) during melting and casting so that the overall EHEA composition remains similar but includes Nb.
drafts.conditions: Processing conditions similar to the original casting and subsequent heat treatments, with performance evaluated under room temperature and elevated temperature conditions (up to ~700°C) as well as in corrosive media (e.g., chloride-containing acidic environments) and under long-term mechanical loading.
drafts.structural_mediator: The Nb addition is anticipated to induce controlled precipitation of fine, coherent Nb-rich phases within the FCC lamella, or at the lamellar interfaces, which serve as obstacles to dislocation motion and also help stabilize the lamellar microstructure during high-temperature exposures.
drafts.mechanism: Nb microalloying facilitates a precipitation-strengthening mechanism. The fine Nb-rich precipitates refine the effective lamellar spacing and reinforce dislocation pinning, which improves yield strength and creep resistance. Simultaneously, they are expected to inhibit coarsening and phase segregation under thermal cycling, thereby also enhancing corrosion resistance by stabilizing the microstructural interfaces.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Nb-modified alloy should exhibit enhanced yield and creep strength (tentatively estimated to improve key metrics by 20–30% relative to the unmodified alloy) along with improved corrosion resistance in aggressive environments, while retaining a favorable balance of ductility.
drafts.baseline: The performance characteristics of the original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA without any Nb addition, which, while promising, are still short of stringent industrial requirements under fluctuating and extreme service conditions.
drafts.boundary: The benefits are expected when processing and heat treatment are closely controlled; excessive Nb content might lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases. The approach is applicable to similar EHEA systems where microalloying is capable of inducing fine precipitation without disrupting the eutectic lamellar morphology.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one group of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with a 1–2 at% Nb addition and one control group without Nb. Use identical casting, thermo-mechanical processing, and heat-treatment protocols for both groups. Subject the samples to tensile testing (at room temperature and up to 700°C), creep testing under sustained mechanical loading, and corrosion evaluations in a controlled chloride-containing acidic solution.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at fracture at various temperatures
Creep rate measurements under constant load at elevated temperatures
Electrochemical corrosion parameters (e.g., corrosion potential, current density) via potentiodynamic polarization tests
Microstructural analysis (TEM, XRD) to verify the presence, size, and distribution of any Nb-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 15% increase in yield strength and a measurable reduction in creep rate, along with improved corrosion resistance) while maintaining comparable ductility relative to the control group, then the hypothesis is falsified.
